rows.verified: HSE defines a confined space as enclosed or largely enclosed with a reasonably foreseeable specified risk to workers.
Specified confined-space risks include fire, explosion, loss of consciousness, asphyxiation and drowning.
Noxious fumes, reduced oxygen levels and fire are identified as core confined-space hazards.
HSE says confined-space tasks should be avoided wherever reasonably possible.
Where entry cannot be avoided, the particular space must be risk assessed and controls planned.
Harmful fumes should be ventilated or removed before or during controlled work.
Where liquids or gases could flood the space, isolation such as locking valves shut should be considered.
If oxygen is insufficient, breathing apparatus or ventilation to increase oxygen must be provided before entry.
Confined-space risk depends on the enclosure, atmosphere, work process, possible ingress, isolation, competence, communications, rescue arrangements and time.
HSE confined-space guidance is space-, task-, atmosphere-, worker-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level harm probability.
The Work at Height Regulations apply where a fall could cause personal injury.
Dutyholders must ensure work at height is properly planned and organised.
People involved in work at height must be competent.
Risks must be assessed and suitable work equipment selected and used.
Risks from fragile surfaces must be properly managed.
Work-at-height equipment must be properly inspected and maintained.
Dutyholders should avoid work at height where possible, including completing work from ground level.
Emergency and rescue arrangements must be planned and should not rely solely on the fire brigade.
Work-at-height risk depends on the task, height, edge and surface condition, equipment, weather, competence, supervision and rescue capability.
HSE work-at-height evidence is task-, equipment-, surface-, worker-, weather-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level fall probability.
